item.title: Bangladesh takes climate justice demand to COP31
item.description:
Bangladesh will press for increased grant-based climate finance, stronger global commitments on adaptation and greater accountability from major polluters at the upcoming COP31 climate summit, seeking international support to tackle worsening climate impacts without adding to the country’s debt burden.
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman is scheduled to attend the two-day World Leaders’ Summit on November 11–12, where he is expected to present Bangladesh’s priorities on climate justice, international financial commitments and support for implementing national climate plans.
The 31st Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) will take place in Antalya, Türkiye, from November 9 to 20. It is expected to bring together world leaders, climate negotiators, development partners, civil society representatives and international organizations.
Bangladesh’s central message is that the countries bearing the greatest climate risks, despite contributing relatively little to global emissions, should not have to take on more debt to protect their people.
Environment, Forest and Climate Change Minister Abdul Awal Mintoo outlined the country’s negotiating priorities at a press conference at the Secretariat in Dhaka on Thursday.
Special Assistant to the Prime Minister for Environment and Climate Change Dr Saimum Parvez, Acting Secretary of the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change Dr Fahmida Khanam, Additional Secretary Navid Saifullah and Bangladesh Climate Change Trust Managing Director Kazi Rawnaqul Islam were also present.
Mintoo said Bangladesh would prioritize climate justice, protection of vulnerable communities and international financial and technological support for implementing its climate commitments. He emphasized the need for adequate, predictable and accessible climate finance, primarily in the form of grants, alongside stronger support for adaptation and addressing loss and damage.
Separately, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam said on Monday that Bangladesh would urge developed countries to provide climate finance as grants rather than loans and take responsibility for their contribution to global carbon emissions. Her remarks reinforce Dhaka’s position that climate finance should reflect the historical responsibility of major emitters and the financial needs of vulnerable developing countries.
Bangladesh has prepared a national position paper through consultations with relevant ministries, government agencies and climate experts. It will also coordinate its negotiating position with the Least Developed Countries (LDC) Group, the Group of 77 and China, and other climate-vulnerable countries.
Climate finance is expected to be one of Bangladesh’s principal priorities at COP31, with Dhaka seeking stronger implementation of commitments made by developed countries under international climate agreements. The country will call for new, additional, predictable and accessible resources to support adaptation, resilience-building and the implementation of national climate plans.
A key demand will be that assistance for climate-vulnerable developing countries should come primarily through grants instead of loans. Bangladesh argues that loan-based climate assistance can increase public debt and place an additional financial burden on countries already dealing with the economic consequences of climate change.
The government will also press for simpler application and approval procedures for international climate funds. Lengthy processes and complex administrative requirements, Bangladesh maintains, can prevent resources from reaching communities when they are most urgently needed.
The issue has wider significance for developing countries as they seek to bridge the gap between the scale of climate action required and the financial support currently available.
Earlier, at COP29 in Baku, countries agreed that developed nations would take the lead in mobilizing at least $300 billion annually for developing countries by 2035, within a broader effort to scale up climate finance from all sources to $1.3 trillion a year by the same deadline. For Bangladesh and other vulnerable nations, the challenge is to ensure that such commitments translate into accessible funding, particularly for adaptation and loss and damage.
Bangladesh will seek greater accessibility and effectiveness of the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, established to assist developing countries particularly vulnerable to the adverse effects of climate change. Dhaka will advocate faster disbursement, simplified funding procedures and stronger support for communities facing irreversible climate impacts.
The country will also raise the importance of addressing non-economic losses, including displacement, disruption of traditional livelihoods and damage to cultural heritage and community identity. These concerns are particularly pressing for coastal and riverine communities in Bangladesh, where erosion, salinity intrusion, cyclones and other extreme weather events threaten homes, livelihoods and habitable land.
The government’s position is that international support must respond to the actual needs of affected populations rather than remain confined to financial pledges that are difficult to access. Bangladesh will therefore seek arrangements that allow vulnerable countries to respond to climate-related disasters while also investing in long-term resilience.
Bangladesh will call on countries to accelerate science-based greenhouse gas emission reductions in line with the Paris Agreement’s goal of limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels.
Dhaka will urge developed countries to demonstrate leadership in cutting emissions and call on major emitting economies to strengthen their climate commitments in line with their responsibilities and respective capabilities. It will also emphasize that developing nations need finance, technology transfer and capacity-building support to implement their nationally determined contributions (NDCs).
For Bangladesh, stronger global mitigation is essential because adaptation alone cannot eliminate the growing risks associated with continued warming. The government will argue that the countries with the greatest historical responsibility and financial capacity must take the lead in reducing emissions while supporting vulnerable nations to pursue climate-resilient development.
Implementation of Bangladesh’s National Adaptation Plan (NAP) will be another major focus of the negotiations. The government will seek financial and technological assistance to strengthen resilience in coastal areas, wetlands, river islands and drought-prone regions.
Priority areas include water security, food production, public health, disaster preparedness and the protection of climate-sensitive livelihoods. Bangladesh will also highlight the importance of early warning systems, climate-resilient infrastructure and locally led adaptation initiatives.
Coastal communities facing cyclones and salinity intrusion, farmers affected by irregular rainfall and drought, and riverine populations confronting erosion and displacement are among those requiring stronger support. Dhaka will press for adaptation finance that reaches local communities and supports solutions shaped by their needs, traditional knowledge and direct experience of climate impacts.
Bangladesh will seek international cooperation to support a just and equitable transition towards low-carbon development across the energy, agriculture, industrial and transport sectors.
The government will emphasize that the costs and benefits of the transition must be distributed fairly, with particular attention to workers, low-income communities, women and young people. Skills development, social protection, labor rights and decent employment opportunities will be important elements of the country’s just transition agenda.
Dhaka will also advocate affordable access to renewable energy technologies, energy-efficient systems, cleaner industrial production and sustainable transport. Its position is that developing economies need international finance and technology to pursue cleaner growth without undermining employment, economic competitiveness or social development.
Bangladesh will explore opportunities to mobilize additional finance and technological support through international carbon markets under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. The mechanism allows countries to cooperate in meeting their climate commitments, including through internationally transferred emission reductions and other forms of cooperation.
Dhaka considers carbon markets a potential supplementary source of finance for implementing its NDCs and supporting low-carbon development. However, the government will maintain that carbon market cooperation cannot replace predictable public climate finance, particularly for adaptation and loss and damage.
Bangladesh will also seek stronger international cooperation on affordable climate technologies, technical expertise and institutional capacity-building. Such support will be important for renewable energy, climate-resilient agriculture, industrial decarbonization, water management and disaster preparedness.
The country will advocate greater international support for conserving forests, mangroves, wetlands and biodiversity as part of its wider climate response. Nature-based solutions can strengthen ecosystem resilience while supporting local livelihoods and sustainable resource management. They are particularly relevant to Bangladesh, where mangrove forests, wetlands and river systems provide protection against climate hazards and support millions of people.
Bangladesh will also emphasize inclusive climate governance and meaningful participation by women, children, young people, persons with disabilities and marginalized communities. The government will seek improved access to climate finance for women-led and locally led initiatives, arguing that climate policies must reflect the needs and experiences of vulnerable populations.
Bangladesh is also expected to raise concerns about climate-related international trade measures that could affect the exports, employment and competitiveness of developing economies.
Dhaka will seek cooperation to ensure that environmental trade policies do not place disproportionate burdens on countries with limited financial and technological capacity. The government will advocate assistance to help industries adopt cleaner technologies, improve energy efficiency and meet evolving international environmental standards.
Its position will be that the shift towards sustainable production should be supported through finance, technology transfer and capacity-building rather than measures that could undermine development opportunities. For Bangladesh, the challenge is to balance global climate objectives with economic growth, employment generation and poverty reduction.
Bangladesh will establish a 100-square-metre pavilion at the COP31 conference venue to showcase its climate vulnerabilities, adaptation experience and national priorities.
The pavilion will feature the country’s updated nationally determined contribution, known as NDC 3.0, alongside its National Adaptation Plan and initiatives addressing climate-induced loss and damage. Other areas of focus will include climate finance, renewable energy, carbon markets, nature-based solutions and technological innovations supporting climate resilience.
The pavilion is expected to provide a platform for policy discussions, knowledge exchange and engagement with international development partners, research institutions and potential investors. Bangladesh also intends to highlight locally developed adaptation solutions and community experiences, demonstrating how people directly affected by climate change are responding to its impacts.
The government hopes the pavilion will help create opportunities for partnerships, technical cooperation and investment aligned with national climate priorities.
Bangladesh’s negotiating position will be guided by equity and the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities, a foundation of international climate cooperation. The principle recognizes that all countries have a role in addressing climate change, but their responsibilities and capacity to act differ according to historical circumstances and national capabilities.
Dhaka will argue that developed countries must fulfil their international commitments while providing vulnerable developing nations with the resources needed to implement climate action. The position also reflects a broader demand for accountability from major polluters, particularly as countries facing severe climate impacts struggle to finance adaptation and recovery.
For Bangladesh, climate justice is not limited to securing financial pledges. It also means ensuring that international support is accessible, reaches affected communities and reflects the scale of the damage they face.
COP31 comes at a critical point for international climate cooperation, with countries under growing pressure to turn existing commitments into measurable action.
Türkiye will host the conference, while Australia will chair the negotiations under the agreed organizational arrangement. Discussions are expected to focus on implementing the Paris Agreement, strengthening adaptation, mobilizing climate finance and supporting a fair transition towards cleaner energy systems.
With Prime Minister Tarique Rahman preparing to present the country’s position at the World Leaders’ Summit on November 11–12, Dhaka will seek to put grant-based finance, climate justice and the protection of vulnerable communities at the center of the discussions.
The success of COP31, from Bangladesh’s perspective, will ultimately depend not simply on new declarations but on whether international commitments deliver practical support to countries and communities already living with the consequences of climate change.

Hasina seeks passport to return, govt insists on extradition
item.description:
Former prime minister Sheikh Hasina has formally sought a new Bangladeshi passport and national identity card to facilitate her planned return from India in December, but the government on Monday made clear that it wants her brought back through the extradition treaty rather than allowing her to return as a traveller.
The development, first reported by Reuters, marks Hasina’s first known formal communication with Bangladeshi authorities since she left for India following the mass uprising in August 2024.
While State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir dismissed the application and insisted on extradition, Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said the government was examining its authenticity, legal basis and procedural validity.
The International Crimes Tribunal’s chief prosecutor, meanwhile, described the move as a political stunt and questioned whether Hasina genuinely intended to return.
According to Reuters, lawyers from London-based Matrix Chambers sent a letter on Monday to Preeti Rahman, acting high commissioner at the Bangladesh High Commission in New Delhi.
The lawyers requested a new passport and NID for Hasina, citing the reported cancellation of her existing documents by Bangladesh’s interim government and other authorities.
They urged the mission to process the applications expeditiously, referring to her Bangladeshi nationality and obligations under international human rights instruments.
Hasina has previously told Reuters that she intends to return to Bangladesh in December and surrender before a court.
The former prime minister was sentenced to death in absentia by the International Crimes Tribunal in November 2025 over crimes against humanity committed during the crackdown on the 2024 student-led uprising.
She has denied the charges.
Responding to the development at the foreign ministry, State Minister Humaiun Kobir described Hasina’s application as “utterly ridiculous.”
He said Bangladesh would not issue an ordinary passport to facilitate the return of a fugitive convicted of serious crimes.
The state minister stressed that Bangladesh and India already had an extradition treaty and that Hasina’s return should be handled under that agreement.
“If she genuinely wants to return to Bangladesh, she should ask the Indian government to hand her over under the extradition treaty,” he said.
Kobir also criticised the British law firm representing Hasina, questioning the legal and ethical grounds for pursuing the application.
He acknowledged that individuals could engage lawyers and submit representations to authorities, but said doing so did not automatically establish entitlement to a passport.
According to media, diplomatic sources also questioned whether the application had been properly authorised, saying the email did not include a signed authorisation from Hasina.
The Bangladesh mission in Delhi forwarded the communication to the foreign ministry.
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed adopted a more procedural position, saying the government was still verifying the reported application.
Speaking to reporters at the Secretariat, he said he had learned about the request through media reports but had not independently confirmed its authenticity.
The foreign and law ministries were examining whether the application had been submitted in accordance with the rules and whether Hasina was legally entitled to apply for the documents, he said.
The review would consider the relevant provisions of passport, citizenship and national identity laws.
Salahuddin reiterated that Bangladesh had already approached India through diplomatic channels seeking Hasina’s return under the bilateral extradition treaty.
He said the government would take the necessary steps after examining the legal issues.
International Crimes Tribunal Chief Prosecutor Md Aminul Islam dismissed the application as an attempt to generate political attention.
“Whatever Sheikh Hasina is doing now is a political stunt. She will not come back,” he told reporters at the tribunal.
He said a formal press conference would be held on Tuesday, November 10, to explain the prosecution’s position on Hasina’s reported willingness to surrender.
The prosecutor’s remarks came as the government continued its efforts to secure the former prime minister’s return to face the consequences of the tribunal’s verdict.

item.title: Tarique-Erdogan meeting in Antalya today as Dhaka-Ankara ties grow closer
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman will meet Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan in Antalya, Türkiye, today, Tuesday.

The two leaders are scheduled to meet at 6:30pm local time at the Maxx Royal Hotel in Antalya. Diplomatic sources in Dhaka confirmed the information to Prothom Alo.

According to diplomatic sources in Dhaka, since the BNP government took office, relations between Dhaka and Ankara have grown closer through reciprocal visits by the two countries' foreign ministers, a visit to Türkiye by the Bangladesh Army chief and high-level contacts. Today's meeting is a continuation of that process.

Prime Minister Tarique Rahman left Dhaka for Antalya this morning to attend the United Nations climate change conference (COP31). During the official visit from 10 to 12 November, the prime minister will lead the Bangladesh delegation. He will deliver Bangladesh's statement at the plenary session of the conference on 12 November.

On the sidelines of the conference, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman may hold bilateral meetings with the leaders of several countries, including the Turkish president.

This will be Tarique Rahman's second meeting with President Erdogan since he took office as prime minister.

The two leaders first met at the Turkish House in New York on 22 September, on the sidelines of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly. At the meeting, Erdogan called for placing bilateral relations on a more institutional footing. He emphasised expanding cooperation in the defence industry and increasing bilateral trade.

In early June, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan visited Dhaka. On the final day of his visit, he paid a courtesy call on Prime Minister Tarique Rahman. During the meeting, Fidan said his visit was the first step towards elevating relations between the two countries to a strategic level.

Following the meeting, the two countries announced the formation of a joint committee at the ministerial level on defence and foreign affairs. The two sides also agreed to hold annual meetings between their foreign ministers and regular meetings involving the foreign and defence ministers.

During his visit to Dhaka, Fidan held a joint press conference with Bangladesh Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman. Khalilur Rahman thanked Türkiye for supporting Bangladesh's bid for the presidency of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly.

Contacts between the two countries in the defence sector have increased over the past few years.

In July, Bangladesh Army Chief General Waker-Uz-Zaman visited Türkiye. During the five-day official visit, meetings focused on the existing friendly relations between the two countries, bilateral defence cooperation, military training, defence technology, cooperation in the defence industry, capacity building and various issues of mutual interest.

Both sides expressed interest in further expanding professional ties, exchanging experiences and strengthening defence cooperation between their armed forces in the future. As part of the visit, the army chief also inspected the operations of several leading defence industry and military technology institutions in Türkiye.

The Rohingya issue also features in Bangladesh–Türkiye discussions. At the meeting in New York, Erdogan praised Bangladesh for sheltering more than one million Rohingya. High-level contacts between the two countries have increased since the BNP government took office in February. Türkiye was represented at the swearing-in ceremony on 17 February by Deputy Foreign Minister Beris Ekinci.

item.title: Economy and reforms: LDC graduation window extended, challenges remain
item.description:
USA-TRUMP-TARIFFS-BANGLADESH-FACTORY

On 29 October 2026, during the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly UNGA), a decision was adopted to grant Bangladesh an additional three years to prepare for its graduation from the Least Developed Country (LDC) category. Consequently, Bangladesh will now potentially graduate from the LDC group on 24 November 2029 instead of 24 November 2026.

This decision accords Bangladesh vital extra time to prepare. It also creates an opportunity to retain international support measures and trade preferences accorded to LDCs for a longer period. However, additional time alone will not eliminate the structural vulnerabilities of the economy. For that, concrete actions and tough decisions are imperative. Bangladesh must leverage this opportunity to execute significant and effective economic reforms.

The UN Committee for Development Policy (CDP) reviews the progress of LDCs every three years based on three criteria: Per Capita Gross National Income (GNI), the Human Assets Index (HAI), and the Economic and Environmental Vulnerability Index (EVI). A country is considered for graduation if it meets the requisite thresholds in two consecutive triennial reviews. Bangladesh met these criteria for the first time in 2018 and again in 2021, prompting the CDP to recommend its graduation from the LDC category.

In view of the severe damage inflicted on the economy and development trajectory by the Covid-19 pandemic, the UN exceptionally granted Bangladesh, Laos, and Nepal a five-year preparatory period. As per the UN General Assembly resolution of 24 November 2021, Bangladesh’s graduation date was initially fixed for 24 November 2026. Under the latest decision, Bangladesh and Nepal have been granted a further three-year extension.

This additional timeframe offers Bangladesh a strategic window to address readiness gaps and implement plans for mitigating post-graduation challenges. During the preparatory phase, certain international support measures and trade benefits available to LDCs may continue under existing rules. However, uniform privileges will not apply across all markets, nor will the duration of these benefits be identical. Therefore, Bangladesh must immediately initiate bilateral engagements with its major trading partners. In particular, it must seek clarity regarding post-graduation tariff rates, rules of origin, and market access conditions.

The burden of enhancing competitiveness cannot rest on exporters alone. If the costs of power, energy, transport, logistics, customs clearance, and financing remain prohibitive, businesses cannot reduce unit production costs unassisted. The government must elevate the quality of these public services, while facilitating access to easy financing, technical advice, skill development programmes, and streamlined product certification systems.

To remain competitive in international markets, relying solely on duty-free access will not suffice. Prolonged port clearance delays, high transport costs, uninterrupted energy shortages, complex customs procedures, low productivity, and a narrow export basket must be addressed urgently. Operational efficiency at ports and in transport networks must be enhanced. Production lead times and costs must be curtailed. International labour rights and environmental standards must be upheld. Concurrently, businesses should be incentivised to produce higher value-added goods. Exporters also require targeted support to comply with rules of origin and technical requirements in global markets.

In this context, trade agreements can play a pivotal role. Bangladesh has already entered into several trade negotiations, notably the Economic Partnership Agreement (EPA) with Japan and the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) with South Korea, both of which represent positive steps forward. However, before signing further agreements, the market dynamics of prospective partner countries, high-potential sectors, and specific contractual terms must be rigorously evaluated.

These agreements should look beyond mere import-export tariffs to encompass trade in services, investment, customs clearance, product standards, rules of origin, digital trade, and technological cooperation. Yet, signing agreements does not automatically equate to success. The true benchmark of success will lie in the extent to which export volumes and investment inflows increase, new technologies are transferred, and domestic enterprises benefit.

Bangladesh’s export basket remains overwhelmingly dependent on ready-made garments (RMG). Diversifying away from this concentration to boost non-RMG exports is critical. Potential exists to expand exports in pharmaceuticals, leather goods, processed agricultural products, light engineering goods, and IT-enabled services. Achieving this requires manufacturing goods to international standards, building a skilled workforce, ensuring uninterrupted power and energy supplies, modernising transport logistics, and reducing the cost of doing business. Furthermore, small and medium enterprises (SMEs) require financial and technological assistance to enable their entry into new export markets.

The burden of enhancing competitiveness cannot rest on exporters alone. If the costs of power, energy, transport, logistics, customs clearance, and financing remain prohibitive, businesses cannot reduce unit production costs unassisted. The government must elevate the quality of these public services, while facilitating access to easy financing, technical advice, skill development programmes, and streamlined product certification systems. Such measures will enable commercial enterprises to adopt modern machinery, conserve energy, minimise waste, and boost productivity, thereby creating new product lines to penetrate wider markets.

Reforming the import tariff regime is equally crucial. A major share of the government’s revenue is derived from import-stage taxes. However, high tariffs and supplementary duties inflate the import costs of raw materials and machinery for export-oriented industries, This in turn drives up production costs and erodes competitiveness in international markets.

That is why, tariff structures must be gradually simplified and rationalised through a clear, medium-term roadmap. Unnecessary tariff slabs should be consolidated, aligning duty structures with production and export needs. However, an abrupt reduction in tariffs could undermine government revenue. To offset this, revenue collection from direct income tax and Value Added Tax (VAT) must be enhanced by broadening the tax base and improving the efficiency of tax administration. Reducing reliance on import taxes will safeguard public spending in critical sectors such as education, health, and emergency infrastructure.

The extension of Bangladesh’s LDC graduation timeline comes at a juncture when the domestic economy has been grappling with multi-year headwinds. Under current circumstances, restoring macroeconomic stability must remain the paramount priority. Controlling inflation, bolstering revenue generation, mitigating external sector pressures, and enforcing good governance in the banking sector are indispensable for stimulating investment and production. Resolving these challenges demands deep-seated structural reforms.

The government’s Smooth Transition Strategy (STS) for LDC graduation must also be rigorously implemented. Its primary objective should be to preserve Bangladesh's export competitiveness, employment levels, and development momentum as LDC-specific preferences are phased out. The extra three years must not be viewed merely as a deferral of the deadline; this period must be utilised effectively to rectify economic vulnerabilities, enhance productivity, and prepare Bangladesh for international competition.

* Fahmida Khatun is an economist and Distinguished Fellow at the Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD)

item.title: Behind Bangladesh’s garment boom, workers cut food, healthcare as wages fall short
item.description:
BANGLADESH-GARMENTS/

Before dawn each day, garment worker Shilpi Khatun cooks over a wood-fired clay stove because her family cannot afford gas, before heading to a factory in Gazipur, an industrial hub on the outskirts of Dhaka.

The 27-year-old is the sole breadwinner in a household where her husband is unemployed and her parents and in-laws depend on her wages.

Rising prices have left Khatun struggling to afford basic necessities despite five years in the garment industry, a frustration shared by thousands of Bangladesh's garment workers who staged protests last week demanding the minimum monthly wage be raised to Tk 30,000 ($242.82) from Tk 12,500.

"Everything costs more now. Rent has doubled, food is more expensive and whatever I earn disappears before the month is over," Khatun said as she gathered leafy greens outside her home to eat with rice for lunch.

Wage pressure mounts

Last week's unrest, some of it violent, forced hundreds of factories to shut down as workers staged protests and clashed with police, who used tear gas and sound grenades to disperse demonstrators.

The government's wage board agreed on 4 November to implement a revised wage structure from December, with workers set to receive their first pay under the new scale in January, but has yet to determine the size of the increase.

Parveen and her two daughters often live on little more than rice and vegetables, with meat and fish becoming luxuries beyond their reach. To cut costs, one of her daughters dropped out of school.

Low labour costs have helped make Bangladesh the world's second-largest apparel exporter after China and a preferred manufacturing base for global brands including H&M, Zara, Gap, Primark and Walmart. The industry generates more than 80 per cent of the country's export earnings and employs more than 4 million people.

Manufacturers, however, say a steep wage increase would erode Bangladesh's cost advantage over rivals such as India and Vietnam and further squeeze margins already under pressure from higher energy costs.

Workers also receive a 9 per cent annual increment and two festival bonuses in addition to their basic wages, manufacturers say, arguing there is limited room for substantial pay increases.

Workers make stark choices

Workers like Khatun say the wage increase has not kept pace with rising prices, forcing them to make difficult choices over everyday spending.

On the hardest days, Khatun's family survives on puffed rice, she said. Sitting in the small tin-shed room she shares with her husband, she said she had not seen a doctor in three years despite worsening health problems.

Her salary has crept up over five years but not enough to match rising costs. She now earns Tk 13,500 ($108), up from Tk 9,000 when she started. With overtime, she earns about Tk 16,000 but the money rarely lasts until the next payday, she said.

Bangladesh has faced a prolonged cost-of-living squeeze since 2022, with inflation averaging around 9 per cent. Food prices initially drove the surge, but non-food costs have remained high.

"I think twice before buying anything, even food," said Roksana Parveen, a 29-year old sewing operator in a factory in Ashulia on the outskirts of Dhaka. "I know my daughters should be eating better, but I just can't afford it."

item.title: Home minister: 316 killed in armed group attacks in CHT over five years
item.description:
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed has said that 316 people were killed in attacks by armed groups in the Chittagong Hill Tracts (CHT) over the past 5 years, including 308 civilians and 8 members of the security forces.
During the same period, 435 civilians and 55 members of the security forces were injured.
The home minister provided the information on behalf of the prime minister in response to a written question from SA Jinnah Kabir, member of parliament for Manikganj-1, during the question-and-answer session on the third day of the fourth session of the National Parliament on Wednesday.
In his question, SA Jinnah Kabir sought information on attacks, abductions, forcible extortion and the use of illegal firearms by armed groups, as well as attacks on members of the army and other law enforcement agencies.
He also asked about incidents affecting the security of Bengalis and people from different small ethnic groups living in the CHT districts of Rangamati, Khagrachhari and Bandarban over the past 5 years, including the number of people killed and injured.
In response, Salahuddin Ahmed said armed groups had carried out 97 attacks on security forces over the past 5 years. During this period, 194 attacks targeted the Bengali community and 81 targeted small ethnic groups.
In addition, 297 people were abducted, forcible extortion was carried out in 471 incidents, and illegal firearms were used in 377 incidents.
Outlining the government's measures to control the security situation in the hill districts, the home minister said the special armed forces operation, "Operation Uttaran", was ongoing to maintain peace and order and suppress terrorist activities.
He said the Bangladesh Army, Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB), police and SRB had increased regular patrols and intelligence activities to prevent terrorist activities.
A strict policy had also been adopted against illegal arms holders, extortionists and terrorists in the hills, he said. Cases were being filed under existing laws over specific allegations of crimes, and the accused were being brought under the law.
The home minister further said regular special joint operations were being conducted by the army, BGB, police and SRB to eliminate the activities of new and old regional armed groups in the CHT and recover illegal firearms.
Based on intelligence information, operations were also being conducted to destroy secret hideouts and training camps of terrorists in remote hilly areas. Helicopters were being used with assistance from the air force when required.
He said the sources and economic sectors linked to terrorists' forcible extortion were being identified and monitored.
To prevent extortion, the number of checkpoints had been increased, while intelligence surveillance of financial transactions, including mobile banking, had been strengthened.
Mentioning that the BGB's capabilities had been increased to prevent the smuggling of illegal firearms and drugs across the border, the minister said surveillance had been intensified in remote areas adjacent to the Mizoram border in India and the Myanmar border.
Police and SRB were also uncovering various sources and networks in the plains involved in supplying weapons and military uniforms, he added.
The home minister further said hundreds of active members of various regional armed groups had been arrested through continuous and special joint operations in the hills.
During these operations, advanced firearms, live ammunition, magazines, combat uniforms, drones and signal equipment used by the groups had been recovered.

item.title: The world’s largest jade mines are fueling Myanmar’s civil war
item.description:
The mountains of Hpakant in northern Myanmar have been gouged into a honeycomb of scars.
Men carrying pickaxes swarm over heaps of earth dumped by mining companies, hunting for rocks that could be worth a fortune.
Hpakant holds the world’s most valuable jade.
For about a decade, Aung Kyaw drove dump trucks at the mines.
The wages were better than anything he could earn at his farm in central Myanmar.
“I needed to pay for my children’s schooling and health care for my mother,” Aung Kyaw, who asked to use a pseudonym because of fears for his safety, said.
But when the military seized power in Myanmar in a coup five years ago, the relative calm in the area came to a halt.
Locals, artisanal miners and community groups turned their focus from the mines to protesting the ousting of a democratic government, while the ethnic guerilla force, the Kachin Independence Army (KIA), fought the military.
“When heavy clashes broke out, Hpakant became completely unstable,” Aung Kyaw said.
As the military cracked down on mass protests, mining operations gradually resumed.
Aung Kyaw returned to Hpakant but he was out of work.
Many small-scale Kachin miners could no longer get permits or were pushed off their land as the military and KIA seized control of more mining land.
But he came across a Chinese businessman looking for a driver who knew the local terrain well enough to take jade north by truck to the border.
Aung Kyaw applied.
The pay was about 700,000 kyat ($477) a trip, more than double his previous mining wage.
He said despite the risk of being killed: “It was a solid income, that’s why I agreed.”
Jade is mostly sold to buyers from China, where it is thought to symbolize purity of spirit and bring good luck.
There are two types of jade: nephrite, which is sourced from numerous countries, and the fine-quality jadeite that comes primarily from Myanmar and can reach prices higher than some diamonds due to the rarity of its finest grades.
Since the coup, more Chinese buyers have been travelling directly to the mines to identify raw stones to be smuggled out, miner Sai Myo Htwe said.
“Once they have collected a large amount, they hand them over to ‘carriers’,” he said, referring to smugglers.
Previously, some jade passed through established markets in Mandalay and the official emporiums in the country’s capital, Naypyidaw, where stones could be taxed and auctioned.
Now, most stones are smuggled directly over the border to China via two main back roads.
Aung Kyaw and other Kachin locals described routes that avoided towns, winding through jungle with steep climbs, mud and boulders, and driving alongside active combat zones.
They said armed men ran checkpoints every 10 to 15 kilometers, some belonging to the KIA and others aligned with the military.
“Whoever is holding the gun, we just pay the fees as instructed by the bosses,”
Aung Kyaw said.
He said the operation was usually split into three legs, coordinated between several drivers and vehicles, with the last leg crossing the N’Mai River.
“While paying your way through checkpoints, if there are active clashes in certain areas, you have to stop wherever you are, and sometimes you even have to sleep overnight in the jungle and wait it out before moving on,” Aung Kyaw said.
Drivers are sometimes ordered to deliver bribes, including premium liquor or parcels, without knowing what is inside, he said.
Last year Aung Kyaw was detained for three days.
He later learned that a regional commander was in dispute with his team’s leadership.
Another driver came under fire in the jungle, surrendered under a white flag and was released only after explaining he worked for a Chinese carrier group, Aung Kyaw said.
His bullet-riddled vehicle had to be replaced.
“Even worse are the unpredictable threats, such as the danger of landmines, getting hit by heavy artillery shells, or facing air strikes,” Aung Kyaw said.
Hpakant is a vast open-pit mining region, with satellite data showing new pits continually opening.
“The miners are literally moving mountains. The quantity of earth is quite staggering,” said International Crisis Group analyst Thomas Kean.
In the first years after the coup, the military held direct control.
But two years ago, the KIA launched a major offensive, capturing large stretches of land along the Chinese border.
Fighting around Hpakant also intensified.
The mines are now divided between the KIA’s political arm, called the Kachin Independence Organization (KIO), and the military, with a contested zone in the surrounding areas.
A 2015 report from international investigative NGO Global Witness estimated Myanmar’s jade production was worth as much as $US31 billion ($45 billion) a year, with 90 per cent of Hpakant-mined jade smuggled into China.
Under Aung San Suu Kyi’s government, officials tried to reform the industry to curb environmental destruction, improve safety, limit the influence of the military and recover tax lost to smuggling.
In contrast, since the coup, jade sales at official auctions have continued, but remain opaque and no central body publishes production records.
“Myanmar’s jade industry is somewhat of an unregulated free-for-all,” the Global Witness report said.
“The industry is worth billions of dollars, but because it’s all smuggled, we don’t have a clear picture of what it is worth,” Mr Kean explained.
“Controlling Hpakant is very lucrative. The biggest change since the 2021 coup has been the direct contest for territorial control, because controlling territory now means controlling the [unofficial] taxation.”
Despite the KIA and military fighting for decades, they also cooperate to share jade profits, entrenching a system of corruption that enriches armed elites while denying local communities the benefits, according to the International Crisis Group.
The ABC tried to contact the Myanmar military and KIA’s top commander but did not receive a response.
Chinese President Xi Jinping has periodically launched anti-corruption campaigns that have temporarily curbed large-scale illicit cash flows used by Chinese businesses to buy unrecorded Myanmar jade.
“The corruption crackdown in China really took the wind out of the market because jade was this store of value if you had a huge amount of cash and you wanted to convert it into something that was portable,” Mr Kean said.
China’s Foreign Ministry has said it is unaware of any allegations of Chinese companies’ involvement in jade smuggling.
The wealth beneath Kachin’s mountains has rarely translated into prosperity for locals.
Hand-pickers can spend days searching for jade and find nothing, leaving them with not enough money for food.
Many migrant workers sleep in cramped tents near unstable slopes, where landslides pose a constant risk.
Small mining plots run by Kachin families were once common.
ND Seng grew up in Hpakant and her brother still works in the mines.
“As a family we would go and look for rocks, and if we found one, we all shared the earnings,” she said, using a pseudonym because of her fears for her brother’s safety.
Since the coup, she said, some Kachin families have been pushed off their plots as conflict between the military and KIA continues, while many migrant workers have decided the safety risks are too great.
Kachin activist May Sabe Phyu said jade had brought more misery than wealth.
“The conflict is more severe. People are displaced again and again.”
Seng Htoi from the Kachin Women’s Association Thailand (Kwat) said the conflict had deepened a wider cycle of lawlessness, including a thriving drug trade.
Aung Kyaw said drugs had become so prevalent that he sometimes relocated from a boarding house to a local monastery, which was itself overcrowded with families fleeing air strikes.
Activists have called for a global ban on Myanmar gemstones.
“There is no way to buy jade from Myanmar and be sure it is ethically traded,” said Min Tent, of Burma Campaign UK.
Justice for Myanmar has urged Australia and other countries to ban gem imports from Myanmar.
“Australia has still not taken any action to target the junta’s revenue from natural resources,” spokesperson Yadanar Maung said.
Unlike some countries, Australia has not imposed sanctions on the state-owned Myanmar Gems Enterprise (MGE) and it is legal to trade jade sourced from Myanmar.
The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade did not comment on MGE but said it condemned the regime’s “brutal and ongoing atrocities” against the people of Myanmar.
DFAT said Australia had sanctioned 21 individuals in Myanmar in response to systematic human rights abuses and the overthrow of democratically elected leaders, as well as five entities involved in funding the regime’s access to weapons and jet fuel.
In the main jade market, China, there is no move to impose a boycott.
“Within China, there’s not the same kind of activists and lobby groups, you don’t have a ‘Free Myanmar campaign’,” Mr Kean said, citing China’s restricted political environment.
“It’s very hard to persuade people, you know, not to buy these products when there is that cultural attachment.”
In Australia, gem dealer Wai Yan said he avoided buying jade from Hpakant and from government-run auctions where sales went to the military junta.
He said he also avoided buying from China for the same reason.
Mr Wai said his company, Mays Gems, instead bought gems from Yangon or Mandalay and “from smaller miners, the families that work around the big corporations.”
“It’s very difficult to source jade, especially from Burma, because of the political situation,” he said.
And he said many customers were more concerned about whether their jade was genuine than about where it came from.
He believed it was possible to ethically buy jade from smaller miners and that his proceeds were not going towards the military.
Fiona Frith, international jewellery director at auction house Bonhams, said most jade pieces it handled came from China, and had been passed down through families with little information about where the stone was originally mined.
“We can’t physically say where something is from by looking at it,” she told the ABC.
She said Bonhams generally steered clear of jade that had a certificate stating Myanmar as the origin, particularly since the coup, putting it in the same category as ivory.
Australian-based Gem Rock Auctions is a marketplace for third-party sellers from around the world. It has several listings of gemstones from Myanmar.
CEO Ross Sedawie said most of the jade traded on the platform was from artisanal miners or had been in the market for a long time and they had travelled to Thailand to meet sellers and verify they were who they claimed to be.
He said believed it was possible to ethically buy jade from Myanmar from artisanal sellers, but that it was getting harder.
His business required verified sellers in Thailand and China to agree to conditions that a sale didn’t benefit a military-linked company or other armed group.
However, ultimately, he acknowledged there was no way to be certain.
“That supply chain is just so hard to police. We just have to take it on face value,” he told the ABC.

UN climate chief urges debt-free climate finance for developing nations
item.description:
UN Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell has called for a fundamental shift in the global climate finance system, urging developed countries, financial institutions and investors to ensure that funding helps developing nations escape mounting debt pressures and build long-term economic resilience.
Speaking at the Seventh Biennial High-Level Ministerial Dialogue on Climate Finance at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, on Friday, Stiell warned that many developing countries remain trapped in a cycle of debt, climate disasters and increasingly expensive borrowing, leaving them with fewer resources to protect their people and economies.
“Climate finance must help countries break free,” he said, stressing that meeting international funding targets alone would not necessarily address the actual financial needs of vulnerable nations.
He argued that climate finance must move beyond funding individual projects towards supporting broader economic transformation, strengthening national institutions and creating conditions that attract more investment at lower costs.
Under the new climate finance goals agreed at COP29, developed countries are expected to take the lead in providing $300 billion annually by 2035, while all actors are expected to work together to scale up financing for developing countries from all sources to $1.3 trillion per year by the same year.
Stiell said the Baku-to-Belém Roadmap provides a pathway towards achieving these targets, but stressed that the way climate finance is delivered must change to make the commitments meaningful.
Explaining the financial challenges facing developing countries, Stiell said the growing threat of floods, wildfires, storms and droughts increases borrowing costs even before disasters occur.
When climate shocks strike, government revenues decline while recovery and reconstruction expenses rise, pushing countries further into debt.
This leaves governments with fewer resources to invest in climate adaptation, resilience and low-emission development, reinforcing a cycle of financial vulnerability.
To break this cycle, he called for climate finance that reflects individual countries' economic circumstances and debt sustainability.
He emphasised that funding must be affordable and tailored to national needs rather than delivered through a one-size-fits-all approach.
While private finance, loans and guarantees remain important for meeting global climate goals, he said grants and highly concessional financing would continue to be essential, particularly for least developed countries (LDCs), small island developing states (SIDS) and other vulnerable economies.
He also called for broader international efforts to address debt burdens so that developing countries are not forced to choose between repaying loans and investing in climate resilience.
Stiell identified easier access to climate finance as another major priority, pointing to the complicated administrative requirements and fragmented funding arrangements that developing countries must navigate.
He said countries often face complex procedures to access funding from multiple programmes and institutions, making it difficult to secure resources when they are needed.
“We need procedures simplified,” he said, calling for stronger coordination among financial institutions and reduced administrative burdens.
He also stressed that international climate finance should align with national development priorities rather than requiring countries to reshape their domestic systems to meet external funding requirements.
National treasuries, local governments, development banks and financial institutions already play important roles in financing development, and these institutions should be strengthened rather than bypassed, he said.
Stiell urged international partners to invest in institutional capacity and help developing countries establish effective systems to access, manage and deploy climate finance.
He also underscored the importance of developing and transferring technologies that support climate-resilient and low-emission development.
The UN climate chief further called for stronger cooperation among governments, climate funds, development banks, financial institutions and private investors to turn national climate plans into tangible investments.
He said climate finance, technology transfer and capacity-building must work together around countries' own priorities, ensuring that funding translates into projects that strengthen resilience and improve people's lives.
As an example, he explained that early grant-based support could help countries build institutional capacity and develop investment pipelines, while concessional finance and risk-sharing instruments could subsequently help projects expand.
He said international climate negotiations and cooperation mechanisms could play an important role in bringing different sources of finance together around national development priorities.
Concluding his remarks, Stiell called for a new approach to international climate finance, saying the biennial ministerial dialogues should help translate commitments into more effective delivery.
Established in 2013, the dialogues have contributed to discussions on global climate finance. However, he said they must now help advance a system that supports long-term development rather than focusing solely on individual funding targets.
“Where every dollar invested in development builds a better future. For all countries,” he said.
His remarks at COP31 highlight a central challenge for developing countries such as Bangladesh: securing not only greater volumes of climate finance but also affordable, accessible and predictable funding that can strengthen economic resilience without deepening existing debt pressures.

item.title: Shahjalal Airport's third terminal to partially open on 16 December
item.description:
The government plans to partially open the third terminal of Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka on 16 December. Initially, the terminal will begin operations with four flights.

Civil Aviation and Tourism Minister M Rashiduzzaman Millat announced this at a meeting on preparations for the inauguration and operation of the third terminal at the conference room of the Civil Aviation Authority of Bangladesh (CAAB) on Saturday morning.

At the meeting, the minister said opening the third terminal was an important commitment of the current government.

The prime minister’s directives must be given the highest priority to ensure that operations begin on schedule. All relevant agencies must complete their respective tasks within the stipulated timeframe.

The meeting discussed various issues, including the activation of the required immigration booths before the terminal opens, installation of baggage belts and scanners, trial operations and signing of agreements.

Representatives of the relevant agencies exchanged views on progress and identified the steps needed to complete the remaining work.

M Rashiduzzaman Millat said the collective efforts of all concerned over a long period had brought the third terminal to the stage where it was ready to begin operations.

He urged the relevant agencies to implement the decisions taken at the meeting on time.

Among those present were Invest Bangladesh Chairman Chowdhury Ashik Mahmud Bin Harun, Dhaka-18 MP SM Jahangir Hossain, Prime Minister’s Special Assistant Gias Uddin, Civil Aviation and Tourism Ministry Secretary Nurunnahar Chowdhury, and National Board of Revenue Chairman Ahsan Habib.

Law minister: Legal process complete for Hasina’s return, India to decide
item.description:
The government has completed all necessary legal procedures to bring back former prime minister Sheikh Hasina, who was sentenced to death in a crimes against humanity case related to the 2024 uprising.
Her return now depends on a decision by the Indian government, Law Minister Md Asaduzzaman has said.
He made the remarks while responding to questions from journalists at the Bangladesh-China Friendship Conference Centre in Dhaka on Saturday.
Asked about Hasina's possible return and the legal steps involved, the minister said Bangladesh had completed the required procedures and the matter was now in India's hands.
On whether Hasina would have an opportunity to appeal, Asaduzzaman said she would not be entitled to do so under the law enacted by Sheikh Mujibur Rahman.
The minister also said the investigation agency and prosecution would soon begin investigations into crimes against humanity in different districts, adding that the government would provide all necessary support.
Regarding the investigation into bringing the Awami League to trial as a political party, he said the government would not interfere in the process.
The investigation agency and prosecution would be allowed to carry out their duties independently, he added.

item.title: Zelensky: US proposes Ukraine cede territory in exchange for joining Nato
item.description:
The United States suggested for the first time that Ukraine cede land to Russia in exchange for joining Nato, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in comments released Saturday, adding that Russia had rejected an energy target ceasefire at talks this week.
Zelensky said Russia was “betting everything” on this winter’s campaign in its war with Ukraine, while warning that the Kremlin’s demands to redraw Europe’s security architecture are “dangerous” and could lead to more wars.
Zelensky spoke to the media Friday after visits to Denmark and Ireland, where he met with European leaders following two days of US-brokered Ukraine-Russia talks in Abu Dhabi.
The talks ended with no breakthrough in Europe’s worst war since World War II, but all sides agreed that European officials should be included in future negotiations.
“The Americans raised a question: ‘What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?’ This was the first time this had been raised,” Zelensky said in the comments kept under embargo until Saturday.
He said Ukraine was discussing “specific security guarantees from Nato and the EU” and that if Western countries confirmed them “then I will ask our Ukrainian society what it thinks: do we accept it or not? I have no right to make that decision on my own.”
US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff attended the Abu Dhabi talks and then met after with Putin and Zelensky separately.
Moscow turned down a proposal for a ceasefire in attacks on energy targets at the Abu Dhabi talks, Zelensky said.
“On the proposal for an energy ceasefire: the Russians don’t want it,” Zelensky said.
Putin’s proposal for a “humanitarian mission” to Kostyantynivka, Zelensky said, was a ploy to get Kyiv to withdraw from the embattled city and open the road to more settlements in the Donetsk region.
Russia said this year that it had seized the town but Ukraine has said fighting is ongoing.
“Putin simply wants us to leave Kostiantynivka so that they can move in and occupy the entire city that way,” Zelensky said.
Moscow’s troops have inched westwards since launching the invasion in February 2022, but have been unable to seize the whole of the Donetsk region.
Zelensky said the EU and Nato are Europe’s “only real security” and that Moscow’s bid to review the continent’s security was “dangerous because... it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations.”

item.title: Ex-Bangladesh PM Hasina to return home despite 'threat of death'
item.description:
Ousted Bangladesh prime minister Sheikh Hasina, sentenced to capital punishment after she was toppled in 2024, told AFP on Monday she would return home in December despite “the threat of death”.

Hasina fled to India in August 2024 after a student-led uprising ended her iron-fisted 15-year rule, and has remained in hiding ever since.

She was sentenced to death in absentia last year after a Bangladeshi court convicted her of crimes against humanity over a deadly crackdown on protesters.

“I am fully aware of the risks I face if I return,” she told AFP in an email interview.

“But I have made my decision, and no threat of death will keep me away from my own country.”

Her insistence on going back comes days after Bangladesh said she would face execution if she returned, adding that she has no further legal recourse after missing the deadline to appeal against her conviction.

The 79-year-old has repeatedly rejected the legitimacy of the trial.

Dhaka has sought her extradition from India, which says the request is under legal review.

Hasina said the stance was “contradictory”.

“For months, they have demanded my return. Yet now that I am taking practical steps to come home, they appear to be more interested in threatening me… than actually allowing it to happen,” she said.

“Frankly, I find these contradictory statements from the Bangladeshi authorities rather revealing.”

‘If death is the price’

Analysts suggest her promise to return is an attempt to remain politically relevant, retain the loyalty of supporters and keep alive a party that once dominated Bangladesh but whose activities are now banned.

She may also be counting on the possibility that the government would find it difficult to execute the daughter of Bangladesh’s founding leader, despite her death sentence.

Hasina denied that her Awami League party was involved in a recent spate of petrol bomb attacks in Bangladesh, as authorities have alleged.

She said she had no intention of seeking India’s assistance to arrange her return.

“Why would I ask another country to extradite me, when I have already decided to return voluntarily?” she said.

“Extradition is a matter between two sovereign states. India will make its own decisions according to its laws, policies and national interests,” she said.

Hasina also faces a string of other charges, including corruption allegations.

“More than 600 false cases have been filed against me,” she said.

Her lawyers had applied for a Bangladeshi passport and national identity card through the country’s high commission in New Delhi, she said.

“I am already making preparations to return to Bangladesh in December,” she said.

“I do not wish to die. I want to live and continue serving my country. But if death is the price I must pay for returning home, I am prepared to face it. “

item.title: How identity politics is redrawing the India-Bangladesh borderlands
item.description:
THE India–Bangladesh borderlands are not simply spaces of territorial contestation. They are landscapes shaped by shared histories, cultural continuities and deeply intertwined human relationships. These borderlands hold a profound place in Bangladesh’s history.

At Baidyanathtala (later renamed Mujibnagar), near the Indian border, the country’s first government took its oath on April 17, 1971. For decades, despite political tensions and an increasingly securitised border, communities on both sides maintained relationships through cross-border marriages, religious practices, trade, shared languages and everyday interactions.

The political meaning of these borderlands extends beyond territorial security and migration management, raising a more fundamental question: who has the legitimate right to belong?

Recent developments in India’s northeastern border states point towards an increasingly troubling politics of identity. Demolition drives in Assam’s Dhubri district targeting villages largely inhabited by Bengali-speaking Assamese Muslims, the normalisation of derogatory expressions such as Miya, and controversies surrounding villagers’ encounters with the Indian Border Security Force in Tripura have raised questions that extend beyond individual incidents. Who is considered an Indian? Why are certain communities repeatedly required to prove their legitimacy?

These questions reveal a changing relationship between territory, identity and citizenship. For people living along the border, belonging is increasingly negotiated through markers that extend beyond legal documentation: their names, language, attire, religious practices and perceived cultural affiliations.

The border, in this sense, is becoming more than a geographical boundary. It is also a political instrument for distinguishing between those who are considered insiders and those who are treated as outsiders.

This is the cartography of othering: the process through which political narratives redraw the social boundaries of belonging, even within internationally recognised national territories.

The problem becomes particularly acute when religious identity is conflated with national allegiance. Bengali-speaking Muslims in West Bengal, Assam and Tripura are frequently situated within political narratives of illegal migration and demographic insecurity.

Migration and citizenship are legitimate matters of public policy. States have the authority to regulate their borders and establish legal procedures. But when an entire community is persistently viewed through the lens of suspicion, the distinction between immigration enforcement and identity-based exclusion becomes increasingly difficult to maintain.

The political influence of the Bharatiya Janata Party in India’s border states has also contributed to a changing political vocabulary around migration, nationalism and religious identity. Polarising and hateful statements by political leaders, particularly those associated with the political leadership of Assam and West Bengal, have contributed to the normalisation of exclusionary narratives, gradually shifting the boundaries of what is considered acceptable in public discourse.

The territorial imagination underlying some political statements is eq­­u­­ally significant. References by Ind­­ian politicians to Chittagong, Noak­hali and Sylhet as territories that should have belonged to India, or as historical mistakes associated with Partition, are not simply rhetorical provocations. They invoke an unfinished geographical imagination in which historical grievance, religious majoritarianism and territorial nati­o­­n­­alism intersect.

Such narratives deserve scrutiny not because every political statement signals an immediate territorial ambition, but beca­use they can reshape how neighbouring societies perceive one another. The consequences of this politics do not stop at the border fence.

For Bangladesh, these developments carry both political and social implications. Social media has become an important arena where statements and incidents from India’s border states are circulated, interpreted and sometimes amplified without sufficient context.

Reports of discrimination or violence can generate legitimate concern, but misinformation and emotionally charged responses can also deepen antagonism within Bangladesh. The result is a transnational politics of suspicion in which developments on one side of the border influence perceptions and political narratives on the other.

In this context, Myanmar’s Rohin­gya crisis offers a crucial warning. The progressive exclusion of the Roh­i­­n­­gya from citizenship, their institutionalised marginalisation and eventual mass displacement demonstrate how the gradual denial of belonging can develop into a profound humanitarian catastrophe. Bangladesh continues to bear the consequences nea­rly a decade after the mass exodus of 2017.

India and Myanmar are fundamentally different political contexts. The comparison, therefore, should not suggest an inevitable repetition of the Rohingya experience.

History, however, offers an important lesson: major crises rarely emerge overnight. They can begin with the normalisation of suspicion, the politicisation of identity and the gradual erosion of a community’s social and legal legitimacy.

Published in Dawn, November 16th, 2026

Climate adaptation funding shortfall puts Bangladesh under pressure
item.description:
Even after 17 years of Cyclone Aila, the homestead of Md Zia Gain and his wife, Shamima Begum, in Mothbari village of Koyra upazila, Khulna, remains submerged beneath the waters of the Shakbaria River.

A nearly three-kilometre-long and 250-metre-wide channel, formed by tidal currents after an embankment collapsed, has swallowed their home. They now live on the slope of the embankment of the river.

The house of Minoti Sana, a woman in her 60's from the same village, also once stood in what is now the middle of the river. Her land has remained unrecovered since Cyclone Aila.

Ismail Gazi, Yunus Ali and Ilias Gazi, along with many other villagers, share similar stories. They lost their homesteads and have been living on the slopes of embankments for the past 17 years.

Natural disasters are nothing new in Bangladesh. However, the loss of homes, rising salinity and shortages of safe drinking water in coastal areas continue to transform people's lives over the long term. How to address these challenges is being discussed at the COP31 climate conference in Türkiye.

The United Nations Environment Programme's (UNEP) Adaptation Gap Report 2026, published ahead of the conference, highlights the shortfall in climate adaptation finance.

How much funding is needed for adaptation?

According to Bangladesh's third Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0), the country needs US$8.5 billion annually to implement its adaptation priorities. The same document estimates that the average annual flow of funding for adaptation in the country stands at around US$4 billion.

This leaves an annual shortfall of US$4.5 billion, equivalent to approximately Tk 561.38 billion (Tk 56,138 crore), at an exchange rate of Tk 124.75 per US dollar.

NDC 3.0 states that Bangladesh's annual adaptation financing requirements could rise to between US$12 billion and US$14 billion by 2035.

At the same exchange rate, this would amount to approximately Tk 1,497 billion to Tk 1,746.5 billion (Tk 149,700 crore to Tk 174,650 crore).

Growing needs, insufficient funding

Bangladesh's National Adaptation Plan (NAP) estimates that the country will need a total of US$230 billion to implement 113 initiatives between 2023 and 2050. This amounts to an average of approximately US$8.5 billion annually over 27 years.

The initiatives cover various sectors, including water, agriculture, fisheries and livestock, urban development, disaster management, biodiversity and institutional capacity-building.

UNEP's report draws its estimate of Bangladesh's annual adaptation financing needs of US$12–14 billion by 2035 from the country's third NDC.

The report also states that international public adaptation finance from developed countries to developing nations stood at US$28.7 billion in 2024, an increase of just US$1 billion from the previous year.

The annual adaptation financing needs of developing countries could reach approximately US$305 billion by 2035. This estimate uses 2024 prices and excludes the requirements of the private sector. Including private-sector needs could almost double the total requirement.

At COP30, countries called for adaptation finance to increase at least threefold by 2035. According to UNEP's estimates, even if this target is achieved, it would meet only 20 to 29 per cent of the potential adaptation financing needs of developing countries.

The nature of the financing also matters. In 2024, loans accounted for 55 per cent of international public adaptation finance for developing countries, while grants made up 44 per cent. Nearly half of the loans came on market-based or non-concessional terms.

Experts say Bangladesh needs more grants and low-interest, long-term financing to meet its adaptation costs without placing further pressure on public debt.

Climate finance expert Haseeb Muhammad Irfanullah told Prothom Alo, "Reports published ahead of the COP conferences help us understand changes in the nature and flow of adaptation finance and provide useful insights for negotiations. However, a significant funding gap remains in the flow of finance from developed to developing countries."

Bangladesh still bears the cost of climate damage

According to UNEP's report, Bangladesh allocated at least US$400 million from its revenue budget to the Bangladesh Climate Change Trust Fund between 2010 and the 2017–18 fiscal year. During this period, the authorities approved 512 projects across 18 ministries.

At least 45 per cent of the fund, or more than US$180 million, went towards adaptation activities. However, this amount remains inadequate compared with the country's potential annual requirement of US$12–14 billion.

The Climate Budget Report for the 2026–27 fiscal year estimates climate-related expenditure of Tk 517.46 billion (Tk 51,746 crore) across 25 ministries and divisions. Of this amount, Tk 389.06 billion (Tk 38,906 crore) is allocated to adaptation.

The national budget also proposes an allocation of Tk 1 billion (Tk 100 crore) for the Bangladesh Climate Change Trust Fund.

However, the overall figure for climate-related expenditure does not represent a separate allocation for new adaptation projects. Rather, it reflects climate-related spending identified within the budgets of various ministries and divisions.

Adaptation can reduce climate risks, but it cannot prevent all losses and damage. In the first funding round of the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, 119 developing countries applied for US$2.8 billion.

However, the fund initially had only US$342 million, equivalent to around one-eighth of the total demand. Complex application procedures and limited institutional capacity also pose barriers to accessing support.

Farah Anjum, Bangladesh country lead at the Global Strategic Communications Council, who is attending COP31, told Prothom Alo, "Although Bangladesh faces significant climate risks, its contribution to global emissions is low. Yet the country has to bear much of the substantial cost of adaptation from its own resources. Developed countries should go beyond their existing commitments and provide accessible grant-based financing, technology transfer and technical assistance. They must also ensure that allocated funds reach vulnerable communities and effectively reduce climate-related losses and damage."
